author: Jon Swartz
title: How Apple Got Upstaged
text:
Joney Ive, Apple’s design chief, and CEO Tim Cook Photo: courtesy of Apple By Jon Swartz Sept. 14, 2018 6:59 p.m. ET Pity the poor tech company that plans major product news the same week as The Apple Event.
Steve Jobs perfected the highly scripted press event to the point that it’s now seemingly the template for every tech company’s product introductions. It’s no coincidence that the rise of big company events coincided with the demise of once-flourishing tech conferences like Comdex (Las Vegas), PC Expo (New York), and Macworld Expo (San Francisco, Boston).
In recent years, Apple has widened the audience for its soiree with a highly-produced live video stream. This year, it distributed the stream beyond its own website and devices, with Twitter carrying the event live. (Twitter declined to comment on how many people watched the Apple event.)
And yet a funny thing happened with Apple’s latest iPhone announcement on Wednesday. Instead of getting out of the way of the $1 trillion company from Cupertino, Calif., the rest of tech leaned in. And, from this columnist’s point of view, Apple (ticker: AAPL) was upstaged.
AT&T (T) laid out plans and progress for 5G. Nvidia (NVDA) announced plans for bringing artificial intelligence to autonomous robots and health care. And HP Inc. (HPQ) announced a 3-D printer capable of mass-producing metal parts.
Newsletter Sign-up “In the grand scheme of things, the future impact of the 5G announcements overshadowed the incremental improvements of the iPhone,” Moor Insights & Strategy President Patrick Moorhead, who attended the Apple event, tells Barron’s. “5G will revolutionize business models and impact just about everybody and every business.”
Here’s a recap of the week and what it will mean over the months to come.
Apple: The meeting may have lacked the wow-factor of past Apple events, but the announcement of three new iPhones and a new Apple Watch still garnered plenty of media coverage.
Apple stock closed down 1.2%, to $221.07 on event day. The big question remains how long Apple can keep up its bulging iPhone act. After pushing its average selling price up $100 in the last year, the company continues to push its pricing strategy. Its largest phone ever—the 6.5 inch iPhone XS Max—is also its most expensive, starting at $1,099 and going all the way to $1,449 (see related story, page 15).
Analysts can’t quite agree on the pricing strategy , but investors seem assuaged. Apple shares jumped the day after the event, finishing the week up 2%.
Apple could retake the lead from Samsung in worldwide smartphone shipments by the end of the year, largely because of the iPhone XS Max, according to Annette Zimmermann, research vice president at Gartner. The market researcher forecasts Apple will ship a record 80 million iPhones in the fourth quarter, after dips in the same quarter both in 2017 (73 million) and 2016 (77 million).
AT&T: On Monday, with San Francisco’s Palace of Fine Arts Theater offering a postcard-perfect setting, AT&T offered further proof that mobile’s next-generation, blur-fast 5G network is slowly taking shape.
The telecommunications giant says its 5G network is mature enough that it’s now placed a call with a handset using an early version of Qualcomm ’s (QCOM) 5G radio chip. AT&T is now planning to roll out some form of mobile 5G services in 12 U.S. cities by the end of the year.
Verizon Communications (VZ), meanwhile, will deliver home internet service via 5G in select cities starting on Oct. 1, marking the first 5G commercial service available in the U.S.
A vast majority of smartphone users won’t see the benefits of the technology first-hand until next year at the earliest, but when they do it is likely to leave an impression. Imagine downloading a movie in seconds or instantly viewing PowerPoint presentations.
AT&T shares, which have slumped the past 12 months over concerns about its recently closed merger with Time Warner, closed the week up 3%.
Nvidia : CEO Jensen Huang flew to Japan for his company’s event on Thursday—perhaps to avoid Apple’s shadow. But from an investor perspective, the Silicon Valley chip maker easily stood on its own. Nvidia announced a new platform for real-time AI-use at data centers that use Nvidia’s Turing graphics chips. The CEO also introduced new chip sets for autonomous robots and medical instruments for tasks such as diagnostic imaging that require heavy-duty data crunching.
In a phone briefing with reporters late Wednesday, Nvidia said the deep-learning inference market would be worth $20 billion in five years. Nvidia said Alphabet ’s (GOOGL) Google has already agreed to deploy Nvidia’s chips in its data centers. Nvidia shares rose 1% to $271.34 on the news and finished the week up slightly.
HP : The largest maker of personal computers and a force in printers on Monday announced a breakthrough in manufacturing with Metal Jet, its first printer capable of mass-producing 3-D metal parts.
“We are in the midst of a digital industrial revolution that is transforming the $12 trillion manufacturing industry,” HP CEO Dion Weisler said. HP shares rose 1% on the news.
Volkswagen (VOW3.Germany) will initially print specialty parts such as customized car key rings and nameplates on certain models.
Tim Greene, an analyst at market researcher IDC, says HP’s approach differs from dozens of other companies offering metal printing because Metal Jet can mass produce parts at “significantly” lower costs.
3D Systems (DDD) and Stratasys (SSYS), once the darlings of the 3-D printing industry, have tumbled over the last four years, largely because of the HP threat.
